title: Create, install, and test structured data safely
owner: Website developer or the person who manages your SEO settings; the business owner checks the facts.
where: The relevant page's SEO or schema settings, or the page template's HTML head.
when: Use this when the page's evidence indicates a structured-data issue, or you have decided appropriate markup is genuinely missing.
steps: Check what is already there first. Open the page source or your website's structured-data settings and look for existing application/ld+json code. If an Organization or business object already exists, edit that object rather than creating a duplicate.

If a suitable business object is genuinely missing, use the example below only as a starting point. Replace the example URL and business name with your real, public details. Delete anything you cannot verify. For a different page type, use a schema type that actually describes that page.

If your website platform or SEO plugin has a structured-data editor, enter the information in its appropriate fields and use its preview. Otherwise, a developer can add the complete script shown below to the correct page template's HTML head. A field that expects JSON only must not receive the surrounding script tags.

Before publishing, back up the existing settings or code. Test the complete page or code in the Schema Markup Validator at https://validator.schema.org/ and fix the specific errors it reports. For types Google supports for rich results, also test https://search.google.com/test/rich-results.

Publish the change, open the real page, check the source or rendered HTML, and test the live URL again. If your site uses a shared business object, verify the one shared change instead of blindly adding a new object to all 25 pages.
verify: The complete intended markup parses, its facts match the visible website, and the relevant validator reports no errors for the object changed.
caution: This is an illustrative placeholder, not your business's code. Replace every placeholder. Valid structured data does not guarantee a Google rich result or an AI citation.
example:
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Organization",
  "@id": "https://example.com/#organization",
  "name": "REPLACE WITH THE REAL BUSINESS NAME",
  "url": "https://example.com/"
}
</script>

title: Work through technical access issues
owner: Website developer or technical SEO specialist, with the owner's approval.
where: The affected URL, website templates, robots.txt, sitemap, and verified search tools.
when: Before substantial content work if a public page may be inaccessible or unintentionally blocked.
steps: For each flagged URL, open the page in a normal browser and note the observed issue. Distinguish a failed fetch from an issue that the audit could not evaluate.

Ask the developer to check the HTTP response, the canonical URL, any noindex directive, and the robots.txt rule for the relevant crawler and path. Keep intentionally private or excluded pages protected.

Confirm that important public content is available in the appropriate initial or rendered HTML. Inspect the relevant canonical URL and XML sitemap entry; a sitemap entry alone does not establish indexing.

For Google, use the verified property's URL Inspection tool to review indexing and request indexing when appropriate. Use a separate performance test, such as PageSpeed Insights, if speed needs evaluation.
After the approved change is published, test the same URL and run the audit again. Record what changed and which result was actually verified.
verify: The intended public page responds, has the intended access rules, and is independently checked in the relevant tool. An audit pass does not prove indexing or rankings.
caution: Do not remove all crawler restrictions, noindex directives, or canonical tags without understanding why they exist.

title: Improve and repurpose a weak content page
owner: Content editor and subject-matter expert; the business owner approves claims.
where: A page flagged for review and the editor used to publish it.
when: After access and technical blockers are addressed; start with a page important to customers.
steps: Read the page's own findings and decide what the visitor is trying to accomplish. A heuristic score is a prompt to review, not proof that a page is bad.
List the genuine questions a visitor would expect this particular page to answer. Check the existing content and confirm facts with a knowledgeable person; add only important missing information.

Rewrite unclear passages without changing their meaning. Use descriptive headings, an easy-to-follow order, and a direct answer where they naturally help. Link claims to reliable sources when appropriate.
Preview on desktop and mobile, publish, and ask an unfamiliar reader to find the answer. Do not add generic FAQs, statistics, or filler just to raise a score.

If the improved material is useful in another format, turn its verified points into a short checklist, social post, email, or video outline. Tailor it to that format, link back to the relevant source page, and have the owner approve it.
verify: A reader can complete the page's intended task, the approved facts are accurate, links work, and any repurposed version matches the source.
caution: Short legal, utility, contact, or transactional pages do not need extra copy simply because a length or transition heuristic is low.

title: Find real keyword and competitor gaps
owner: Website owner or marketing specialist; use only data and accounts you are authorized to access.
where: Your verified Google Search Console property, genuinely inspected competitor pages, and licensed keyword data if available.
when: When those separate sources are available. This website audit alone does not measure competitor rankings, search volumes, or actual AI citations.
steps: In your verified Google Search Console property, open Performance and review the queries and pages for the relevant date range. Note the site's own clicks, impressions, and average position; this does not reveal competitor rankings.

Choose genuine competitors or comparable public pages and inspect their visible topics, questions, and page purpose. Record each URL and observation; do not call a topic a gap unless you have actually compared it with your own relevant page.

If you have licensed competitor or keyword data, record its source, region, date, and definitions before comparing rankings or search volumes. Without that data, label those measurements unavailable rather than estimating them.

Select one relevant, supportable opportunity. Update an existing appropriate page or plan a new one only if it serves a real visitor need. Record the intended page, owner, action, and source of the observation.

After publishing, monitor your own Search Console trends over an appropriate period and recheck the public pages or licensed data separately. Note that other changes and seasonality can affect results.
verify: Every claimed gap is traceable to an inspected source or licensed dataset; unavailable metrics remain explicitly unavailable.
caution: This guide is a method for collecting evidence, not a claim that this report discovered a competitor or keyword gap.
